account:
Today has contained several oddly uninformative appointments and conversations. My appointment book sent me to the mill for a grain inspection, but the secretary could find no named organizer in the records. No council letters were delivered for the council-letters appointment, and the town's account ledgers still have not been located. These could be ordinary failures of coordination, but together they make me wonder whether my schedule is keeping me occupied without telling me much.

There has been vague talk of a bridge or port change at the bakery. I have not seen any such alteration or established that a proposal exists. I failed to find the baker during my earlier visit. Later I personally heard the baker say that exact quantities and any agreed payment were not remembered, that there was no town charge, and that future orders needed an agreed price. I also heard Townsfolk 28 say the builder had carried a sack of bread at market. That suggests some bread-related activity worth asking about, but neither its purpose nor a connection to the rumours is established.

At tea, my neighbour said there had been chats with several neighbours at the warehouse and invitations to visit. The neighbour denied firsthand knowledge of bridge or port alterations, and did not give me names or a definite plan in the replies I heard. My secretary came to the cottage while still seeking the baker and asked about the rumours and ledgers. I have received no substantive findings from that inquiry.

The clearest unusual arrangement is my eighteen-hundred appointment with the innkeeper in the great hall: I expressly agreed not to arrive early, and its purpose was not stated to the secretary. Combined with warehouse conversations, invitations, and possible bread supplies, it could be preparations for a private gathering or surprise, perhaps involving the innkeeper, neighbour, baker, and builder. That is only a hypothesis, not evidence of wrongdoing or even of a coordinated plan. I am now waiting in my office and intend to honour the appointment without entering the great hall early.
